notes.meaning: Peter tells Christian wives to submit to their own husbands. To submit means to willingly follow his lead, and this holds even if the husband does not believe. The hope is that such a husband will be won to Christ without lectures, simply by watching his wife's pure and respectful life. This is owed to her own husband, not to men in general, and it stops where obeying would mean sinning.

Peter is not banning nice hair, jewelry or clothes. If he were, he would be banning clothes too. He means a woman's real beauty should not come from these things. True beauty is on the inside: a gentle and quiet spirit that does not stir up trouble and stays calm when wronged. That beauty never fades, and God treasures it.

differ.view: Early Methodist teaching took these words as a real ban on curled hair, gold ornaments and costly or showy clothes for Christians.

notes.meaning: The godly women of old trusted in God. They adorned themselves with this inner beauty and with respect for their husbands. Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him "lord," a word of honor (Genesis 18:12). Christian women become her daughters by faith when they do what is right and do not let fear, such as threats from an unbelieving husband, push them off course.

Husbands must live with their wives with understanding and treat them gently. A wife is called the "weaker vessel" because she is physically weaker, not lesser in mind or spirit. She is to be honored as an equal heir of eternal life. Quarrels between husband and wife get in the way of their prayers.

Now Peter speaks to all believers. They should agree in the faith and feel one another's joys and sorrows. They should love each other as family, be tenderhearted toward those who are hurting, and think humbly of themselves. Pride is one of the quickest ways to break friendships.

Christians must not take revenge, either in deeds or in words. Instead they should bless those who hurt them, which means praying for them and speaking well of them. God called them to live this way, and He has promised them a lasting blessing as their inheritance.

Peter backs this up with words from Psalm 34. Whoever wants a good life must keep his tongue from evil and lies. He must turn from wrong, do good, and chase after peace even when it seems to run away. God watches over the righteous and hears their prayers, but He sets His face against those who do evil.

As a general rule, people who are eager to do good are not harmed, because kindness tends to soften even hard hearts. Peter means this as a usual pattern, not a promise of no trouble at all. The next verse makes that clear.

Even if believers do suffer for doing right, they are blessed, just as Jesus said in Matthew 5:10. Peter borrows words from Isaiah 8:12. Do not be terrified by the threats of enemies, and do not be shaken.

Instead of fearing people, honor Christ as the holy Lord in your heart and trust Him fully. Be ready to explain to anyone who asks why you have hope. Answer gently and respectfully, with reverence for God, not proudly or angrily.

Keep a clear conscience, one that does not accuse you of doing wrong. Words without a matching life carry little weight. When your conduct as a follower of Christ is plainly good, those who slander you will end up ashamed.

If God allows suffering, it is far better to suffer for doing good than for doing wrong. A believer's suffering does not come by chance. It comes under God's wise will. Someone who suffers because of his own sin has no such comfort.

Christ suffered for sins once for all, meaning it never needs to be repeated. The innocent One died in place of the guilty to bring us back to God. He was put to death in His human body but was raised to life by the Spirit. His example shows that suffering for doing good leads on to glory.

Christ, by His Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah's day while the ark was being built. God waited patiently, about 120 years, for them to turn back. They refused, and their spirits are now in prison awaiting judgment. Only eight people were saved, carried safely through the water in the ark.

differ.view: Christ, alive after His death, went down to hell to announce His victory over death and the devil, and this verse is the clearest teaching of it.

Many think Christ most likely preached through Noah and did not go to hell after dying, since His saving work was finished on the cross. Some admit the passage is unclear. Calvin read it as Christ's grace being made known to the souls of godly people who had died waiting for Him.
Christ announced His victory to fallen angels imprisoned for the sins of Noah's time (compare 2 Peter 2:4-5 and Jude 6).

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Christ's soul went to the realm of the dead as Savior. He brought the good news to the righteous who were waiting there and set them free. He did not free the lost.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have guessed that an early copyist accidentally dropped a name, so that the verse first said Enoch preached to these spirits. No manuscript supports this.

notes.meaning: The water of the flood is a picture of baptism, which now saves believers. It does not save by washing dirt off the body. Baptism is the outward sign of an inner cleansing, joined with a sincere pledge of a clear conscience toward God. Its saving power comes from the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

differ.view: Baptism does not create new life. It expresses faith already present. Christ is the true ark, and Peter qualifies his words at once so no one thinks the water itself saves.
The ceremony does not save automatically. Trust in Christ saves. Yet the sign should not be torn away from what it points to, which is cleansing by Christ's blood.
God truly gives salvation as a free gift in, with and through baptism. He is acting through His Word and the water.
Through baptism we are saved from the flood of sin, yet not by the bare outward sign but by the inward grace it stands for.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: As described by a Baptist writer, Catholic teaching holds that baptism washes away sin, gives new life, and brings a person into the church, actually doing what it pictures.

notes.meaning: Jesus has gone into heaven and sits at God's right hand, the place of highest honor and power. Angels and all other powers are under His rule. He suffered for doing good, then triumphed. So His suffering followers can also hope for glory after their trials.
